provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall lexis and structure concepts from SSS 2.
The students should be able to identify key components of essay writing.
Introduction:
We have learned various aspects of English language in SSS 2 including vocabulary, grammar and composition.
Today we will review these topics to strengthen our foundation for SSS 3 work.
Content:
Lexis and structure warm up will cover common vocabulary words and their usage in sentences.
We will review parts of speech including nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
Essay writing review will focus on structure, introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion.
We will examine sample essays to identify strengths and areas for improvement.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify and correct grammatical errors in given passages.
Evaluation questions:
What are the main parts of speech in English?
How many paragraphs should a standard essay contain?
Identify two synonyms for the word 'happy'.
Summary:
Today's lesson has refreshed our knowledge of key English language concepts from SSS 2.
This revision will help us build more advanced skills in our final year of secondary school.

topics.title: Comprehension: summary skills
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify main points in a passage.
The students should be able to write concise summaries in their own words.
Introduction:
We have previously read and analyzed various texts in our English studies.
Today we will focus on extracting essential information and summarizing passages effectively.
Content:
Summary skills involve identifying key ideas and supporting details while eliminating unnecessary information.
We will practice different techniques for summarizing including highlighting main points and creating topic sentences.
Passage drills will involve reading texts from various sources including newspapers and literature.
We will learn to distinguish between main ideas and supporting examples.
Class activity:
Students will read a passage about the importance of education in Nigeria and write a summary of 50 words.
Evaluation questions:
What are the three key elements of a good summary?
How long should a typical summary be compared to the original passage?
Summarize the passage about the harmattan season in three sentences.
Summary:
Summary skills are essential for comprehension and will help us in all sections of our English examination.

topics.title: Lexis: antonyms and synonyms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify synonyms and antonyms in given contexts.
The students should be able to use synonyms and antonyms appropriately in sentences.
Introduction:
We have studied various vocabulary words and their meanings throughout our English education.
Today we will focus on words that have similar meanings (synonyms) and opposite meanings (antonyms).
Content:
Synonyms are words that have similar meanings such as 'big' and 'large' or 'happy' and 'joyful'.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings such as 'hot' and 'cold' or 'good' and 'bad'.
We will examine common word lists that appear in WAEC examinations.
Students will practice using synonyms and antonyms in sentences to improve their vocabulary range.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create a chart of synonyms and antonyms for common words like 'beautiful', 'fast', and 'small'.
Evaluation questions:
Give two synonyms for the word 'brave'.
What is the antonym of 'generous'?
Complete the sentence: The weather was very _____ (opposite of warm) during the harmattan season.
Summary:
Expanding our knowledge of synonyms and antonyms will improve our expression and comprehension skills in English.

topics.title: Structure: clause types
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between main and subordinate clauses.
The students should be able to construct sentences using different clause types.
Introduction:
We have previously studied sentence structure and parts of speech in our English lessons.
Today we will examine how clauses work together to form complex sentences.
Content:
A main clause can stand alone as a complete sentence and contains a subject and a predicate.
A subordinate clause depends on a main clause for its meaning and often begins with words like 'because', 'although', or 'when'.
We will practice identifying different types of subordinate clauses including noun, adjective, and adverb clauses.
Students will learn how to combine main and subordinate clauses to create varied and interesting sentences.
Class activity:
Students will be given a set of simple sentences and asked to combine them using appropriate subordinate clauses.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between a main clause and a subordinate clause?
Identify the subordinate clause in this sentence: 'Although it was raining, we went to the market.'
Write a sentence containing an adverb clause of time.
Summary:
Understanding clause types helps us to construct more complex and sophisticated sentences in our writing.

topics.title: Essay: argumentative
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to structure an argumentative essay effectively.
The students should be able to present counter-arguments in their essays.
Introduction:
We have written various types of essays including narrative and descriptive compositions.
Today we will focus on argumentative essays which require us to present and defend a particular viewpoint.
Content:
An argumentative essay typically has an introduction stating the thesis, body paragraphs with supporting evidence, and a conclusion.
Each body paragraph should focus on one main point with examples and explanations.
Counter-view practice involves acknowledging opposing arguments and refuting them with logical reasoning.
We will examine sample WAEC argumentative essays to identify effective techniques.
Class activity:
Students will choose a topic like 'Should students be allowed to use mobile phones in school?' and write an argumentative essay.
Evaluation questions:
What are the three main parts of an argumentative essay?
How should you address opposing views in your essay?
Write a topic sentence for an argument about the benefits of reading.
Summary:
Argumentative essays require careful planning and logical reasoning to convince the reader of your position.

topics.title: Letter: formal and semi formal
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between formal and semi-formal letters.
The students should be able to write letters following WAEC format requirements.
Introduction:
We have studied various types of written communication in our English language course.
Today we will focus on formal and semi-formal letters which are common in WAEC examinations.
Content:
Formal letters follow strict conventions including sender's address, date, recipient's address, subject, salutation, body, and complimentary close.
Semi-formal letters are similar but may use slightly less rigid language and format.
We will examine WAEC format requirements for both types of letters.
Students will practice writing letters on topics such as job applications, complaints, and invitations.
Class activity:
Students will write a formal letter to the principal requesting permission to organize a cultural day event.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between formal and semi-formal letters?
List the essential parts of a formal letter.
Write an appropriate salutation for a formal letter to a business person.
Summary:
Mastering letter writing formats will help us score well in the continuous writing section of our examination.

topics.title: Oral: vowels and consonants
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify and pronounce all vowel and consonant sounds in English.
The students should be able to distinguish between similar sounds (minimal pairs).
Introduction:
We have previously studied the English alphabet and basic pronunciation.
Today we will focus on the individual sounds (phonemes) that make up spoken English, particularly vowels and consonants.
Content:
English has 20 vowel sounds which can be short, long, diphthongs, or triphthongs.
There are 24 consonant sounds including stops, fricatives, affricates, nasals, approximants, and liquids.
We will practice producing each sound correctly with proper mouth position and airflow.
Minimal pairs are words that differ by only one sound such as 'ship' and 'sheep' or 'bat' and 'bet'.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to practice minimal pairs and identify the differences in pronunciation.
Evaluation questions:
How many vowel sounds are there in English?
Give an example of a minimal pair for the /θ/ and /ð/ sounds.
Identify the vowel sound in the word 'cat'.
Summary:
Mastering vowel and consonant sounds is essential for clear communication and success in the oral English examination.

topics.title: Oral: stress and rhymes
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify and use correct word and sentence stress.
The students should be able to identify and produce rhyming patterns.
Introduction:
We have studied individual sounds in English language pronunciation.
Today we will focus on stress patterns and rhymes which are important features of spoken English.
Content:
Word stress involves emphasizing certain syllables in words, which can change meaning as in 'REcord' (noun) and 'reCORD' (verb).
Sentence stress emphasizes important words like nouns, verbs, and adjectives while reducing less important words.
Rhyme identification involves recognizing words that share the same ending sounds, commonly used in poetry and songs.
We will practice identifying stress patterns in various words and sentences.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create short rhyming poems using words related to Nigerian culture and daily life.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between word stress and sentence stress?
Give two words that rhyme with 'light'.
Identify the stressed syllable in the word 'important'.
Summary:
Understanding stress and rhymes will improve our oral English skills and performance in the oral examination.

topics.title: Objective drills
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer lexis and structure questions accurately.
The students should be able to identify and correct errors in given sentences.
Introduction:
We have studied various aspects of English language including vocabulary, grammar, and composition.
Today we will practice objective-type questions which form a significant portion of our examination.
Content:
Lexis questions test vocabulary knowledge including synonyms, antonyms, word formation, and idiomatic expressions.
Structure questions focus on grammar including tense, agreement, sentence structure, and punctuation.
Error analysis involves identifying mistakes in sentences and understanding why they are wrong.
We will practice with past WAEC questions to familiarize ourselves with the examination format.
Class activity:
Students will work in teams to complete a set of lexis and structure questions within a time limit.
Evaluation questions:
Identify the error in this sentence: 'She don't like reading books.'
What is the plural form of 'child'?
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: 'The weather was very _____ during the harmattan season.' (cold/coldly)
Summary:
Regular practice with objective questions will improve our speed and accuracy in the examination.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply all learned concepts in examination conditions.
The students should be able to evaluate their performance and identify areas for improvement.
Introduction:
We have covered various topics in English language throughout this term.
Today we will revise key concepts and practice with past WAEC examination papers.
Content:
Past paper one will include multiple-choice questions on lexis, structure, and oral English.
We will practice timing ourselves to simulate examination conditions.
Marking and correcting will involve identifying mistakes and understanding the correct answers.
We will focus on common errors made by students in previous examinations.
Class activity:
Students will complete a past WAEC paper one under timed conditions and then mark their work in class.
Evaluation questions:
What are the three sections of WAEC English Language paper one?
How much time should you allocate to each section in the examination?
Identify one common error made by students in lexis questions.
Summary:
Today's revision and practice will help us prepare effectively for the upcoming WAEC examination.
